The Witten Index and N = (2, 2) Worldsheet Eﬀective
Theory of Non-Abelian Vortices
Soumyadip Nandi
∗
August 2026
Abstract
The Witten Index for the worldsheet theory of BPS cosmic strings in N = 2
supersymmetry gauge theories have been investigated. Starting from N = 2
supersymmetry alegbra with central charges, BPS bounds and representation theory
of short multiplets has been reviewed. Cosmic strings of codimension 2 is used as
the foundation for constructing the moduli space of the vortex solutions for both
abelian and non-abelian U (N) gauge theories. Major focus has been devoted to
calculating the zero-modes of the vortex moduli. For the non-abelian case, the
vortex moduli space acquires an internal orientational structure described by the
compact CP
N−1
, arising from color-ﬂavor locking. The low-energy dynamics of the
worldsheet is governed by an N = (2, 2) sigma model with the target space
M
vortex
= C × CP
N−1
. Using supersymmetry localization, it is shown that the
Witten index of this worldsheet theory, receives the entire non-trivial contribution
from CP
N−1
. The fermionic/odd contributions of the ground state vanish by virtue
of the Betti Numbers. The main result demonstrates that the index is a topological
invariant, protected by the BPS condition. This provides a non-perturbative link
between the bulk topological defect and the worldsheet supersymmetric quantum
mechanics.

1 Introduction
The interplay between supersymmetry and topology has produced some of the most robust
results in Quantum Field theory. An important example is the Witten Index - the trace
Tr(−1)
F
e
−βH
over the Hilbert space of supersymmetric theory. The Witten index , [1] counts
the diﬀerence between fermionic and bosonic ground states. Because non-zero energy states,
E ≥ 0 cancel in bosonic-fermionic pairs, the Witten index is invariant under continuous
deformations of parameters. This feature, makes the Witten index a particularly powerful tool
for extracting non-perturbative information about strongly coupled systems.
For supersymmetric theories, with topological solitons (defects) , this invariance acquires a
geometric interpretation. The moduli space which can be described as the space for
degenerate minimum energy conﬁgurations, often carry non-trivial topology. The Witten
index of the eﬀective worldsheet theory becomes a characteristic number (integer) of this
space. This connection is particularly essential for BPS objects , [2] , [3] where the central
charge bound [4], ensures that the tension / mass of the vortices is protected against
quantum corrections and the moduli geometry is exact.
Cosmic strings (codimension 2) that arises from spontaneously broken gauge symmetries
provide the foundation for this connection. In N = 2 supersymmetry theories in (3 + 1)
dimensions, BPS cosmic strings preserve half of the bulk symmetry (4 out of the 8
supercharges) leaving an N = (2, 2) supersymmetric eﬀective theory on their (1 + 1) -
dimensional worldsheet. The bosonic zero-modes correspond to the collective co-ordinates on
the vortex moduli space. The translational modes parameterize the position in the transverse
plane and the internal modes are associated with the orientation of the vortex in color-ﬂavor
space. For n non-Abelian vortices in U(N) gauge theories with N
f
≥ N ﬂavors, the two
moduli are the position and orientation in the plane. One complex co-ordinate C encodes
position, the complex space CP
N−1
– a compact Kähler manifold encodes orientation.

This result embodies several notable features. The non-compact C factor, parameterizing the
center-of-mass of the vortex contributes trivially to the index. This reﬂects the fact that the
index is a non-compactly supported invariant. By Hodge theory, the harmonic forms of the

The paper is organized as follows:- Section 2 and 3 reviews the N = 2 algebra and BPS

theorem by allowing fermionic generators. Consequently, beyond the bosonic Poincare

These central charges commute with every generator of the algebra and play an essential role

possibilities and forces any additional bosonic operator on the right-hand side of {a, a} to
commute with the entire Poincaré algebra. Such operators are precisely the central charges.

Remark 2.2 (Origin of the central charge). The central charge originates from the requirement
that the supersymmetry algebra close. In theories with topological solitons (such as cosmic
strings), the commutator of two supercharges acting on a ﬁeld conﬁguration with non-zero
magnetic ﬂux produces a term proportional to the magnetic charge—this is the central charge.

Deﬁnition 3.1 (BPS state). A state |Ψ⟩ is called a BPS state if it saturates the BPS bound ,
i.e., M = |Z|.
This formula is remarkable. Even before considering a speciﬁc example, recall that the central
charge Z is some combination of conserved charges in quantum ﬁeld theory. We learn that the
masses of particles are bounded by their charges. This is known as the BPS bound
3.1 Representation Theory: Long and Short Multiplets
The representation theory of this algebra depends crucially on whether m > |Z| or m = |Z|.
Long multiplets. If m > |Z|, both a
†
α
and b
†
β
act as creation operators. The result is a
multiplet comprising 16 states. This is known as a long multiplet. More generally, for N
supersymmetries, long multiplets contain 2
2N
states.
7
Short multiplets. What is more interesting is what happens when m = |Z|. In this case,
half of the creation operators do not create anything. For example, when m = Z, the b
α
operators must vanish on all states in the multiplet. Only a
†
α
act as creation operators. The
result is a vector multiplet with 4 states, but now with mass m = Z. This is known as a short
multiplet.
For m > |Z|, all four fermionic oscillators aee non-null, and the multiplet is generated by four
independent fermionic creation operators. The resulting long-multiplet therefore consists of 16
states. At the BPS bound, m = |Z| , one eigenvalue of the supersymmetry operator vanishes,
rendering two of the four fermionic operators null. Only two independent creation operators
are left and the multiplet shortens to 2
2
= 4 states. Thus , the 1/2 BPS shortening reduces
the 16 - state long multiplet to 4 state short multiplet..
Therefore, BPS states can be deﬁned as the states that saturate a lower bound on their energy
derived from the supersymmetry algebra and, as a consequence, they belong to shortened
(smaller) multiplets that are protected against quantum corrections.
3.2 Classiﬁcation of BPS States
As mentioned above, a state |Ψ⟩ is called a BPS state if it saturates the BPS bound M = |Z|.
Such a BPS state must satisfy Q |BPS⟩ = 0 for the choice of auxiliary vectors that optimize
the inequality. This means that a subset of the supercharges annihilate the BPS state. The
number of annihilated supercharges depends on the type of bound saturated, leading to the
following classiﬁcation:
•
1
2
BPS (as discussed previously): Exactly half the supercharges annihilate the state. In
N = 2 with 8 supercharges, 4 are preserved and 4 are broken. The resulting
supermultiplet has half the number of states of a generic (long) multiplet.
•
1
4
BPS: Only a quarter of the supercharges annihilate the state. This occurs in
extended supersymmetry (N ≥ 4) or for special conﬁgurations where multiple central
charges are simultaneously saturated.
•
1
2
BPS objects of co-dimension 2 : A cosmic string (topological defect) is a
1
2
BPS
object. It preserves 4 of the 8 supercharges. The broken 4 supercharges give rise to 4
fermionic zero-modes on the string worldsheet (a diagrammatic representation of a
vortex worldsheet is given below), which then reorganize into 2 left-moving and 2
right-moving worldsheet fermions of the N = (2, 2) algebra in 1+1 dimensions.
Proposition 3.2 (Short multiplet). A
1
2
BPS state in N = 2 supersymmetry belongs to a
short supermultiplet of dimension half that of a long multiplet, and its mass (or, for an
extended object, its tension) is exactly equal to the magnitude of the central charge: T = |Z|.
Proof. When M = |Z|, the positive operator Q
†
Q has zero eigenvalues, meaning that there
exist states annihilated by Q. The annihilated supercharges pair bosonic and fermionic states
within the multiplet, halving the number of independent states. For an extended object such
as a cosmic string, the tension T (energy per unit length) plays the role of mass in the bound,
giving T = |Z| for a BPS cosmic string.

4 Topological Defects
Deﬁnition 4.1. A topological defect in a ﬁeld theory with vacuum manifold V is a ﬁeld
conﬁguration φ(x) that is topologically non-trivial i.e, it cannot be continuously deformed to
the vacuum conﬁguration φ = φ
0
. This defect is classiﬁed by an element of a homotopy group
π
(d)
(V), where d is related to the codimension of the defect.
The codimension of the defect determines it’s dimensionality. A defect of co-dimension d in a
D-dimensional spacetime has a worldvolume of dimension D − d . The classiﬁcation proceeds
via the homotopy of a vacuum manifold: point defects (monopoles, codimension 3), are
classiﬁed by π
(2)
(V), line defects (cosmic strings , codimension 2) by π
(1)
(V), domain walls
(codimension 1) by π
(0)
(V), and textures (codimension 0) by π
(3)
(V)
Remark 4.2. The topological deﬁnition guarantees the stability of the defect against
continuous deformations. No local perturbation can unwind a topological defect ; it can only
be destroyed by a phase transition in which the vacuum manifold V itself changes topology.
This stability is the deep reason why topological defects carry protected information that
survives quantization - a property which is going to be essential when we compute the Witten
index of the defect sector.
4.1 Why Cosmic Strings ?
Cosmic strings are the natural test case for our Witten index analysis for several reasons.
First, they are well-understood BPS objects with a rich but tractable moduli space (Section
3). Second, their worldsheet inherits supersymmetry from the bulk (Section 8), providing a
natural setting for the Witten index computation. Third, they are codimension-2 defects,
which means the worldsheet is (1+1)-dimensional and the Witten index machinery of
9
supersymmetric quantum mechanics and sigma models applies directly. Finally, the
non-Abelian generalization produces a worldsheet theory with a non-trivial target space
topology, yielding a non-zero Witten index.
5 Moduli Vortices
In 4D theories, vortices are string like objects that carry magnetic ﬂux which is threaded
through their core. Therefore, a vortex moduli space is the space of all equivalence classes of
vortex solutions to speciﬁc gauge ﬁeld equations ( such as the Abelian Higgs Equation) on a
Riemannian surface or a Kähler manifold.
The moduli space for BPS vortices arises from the degeneracy of minimum energy ﬁeld
conﬁgurations that solve the ﬁrst order of Bogomol’nyi equations. Let’s try and understand
how it works. The Abelian Higgs model is U(1) gauge theory with a complex scalar ﬁeld Φ
that admits topological vortex solutions known as Abrikosov–Nielsen–Olesen (ANO) [11]
, [12] vortices. These are ﬁnite energy, string like defects that arise from Spontaneous
Symmetry Breaking. These are characterized by the quantized magnetic ﬂux and topological
winding. The Lagrangian density in either (2 + 1) or (3 + 1) dimensions, [13], [14] is:-

The Euler Characteristic is topologically invariant , [29] which means that it does not change
under continuous deformations. For orientable compact surfaces, X = 2 − 2g , where g is the
genus, (number of handles). For a circle, X = 2 and for a torus, X = 0.
The alternating sum is crucial here. This means that the even dimensional holes contribute
positively and the odd-dimensional holes contribute negatively. When the odd betti numbers
vanish, as on CP
N−1
, the sum reduces to a simple count of even dimensional cohomology
classes. The reason why odd Betti numbers vanish on CP
N−1
is because it admits a cell
decomposition with exactly one cell in each even dimension 0, 2, 4...(N −1) and no cells in odd
dimensions, [28]. Because cellular co-homology computes H
p
from the cell structure, and
there are no cells in the odd dimension, the odd cohomology groups vanish identically.

= 0 for all k.
This is a general property of complex manifolds with a cell decomposition into even
dimensional cells, which includes all the complex Grassmannians. It is not automatic for
arbitrary manifolds; it reﬂects the underlying complex structure.
Remark 6.5 (Kähler Manifold and Hodge Theory). CP
N−1
is not just a complex manifold; it
is Kähler , meaning that it carries a closed non-degenerate (1, 1) form. Hodge theory , then
deﬁnes the cohomology decomposition. [30]
If you recall, the Kähler manifold is a special kind of manifold where the complex structure,
the metric and the notion of the area are all perfectly compatible. On an ordinary complex
manifold, you only know how to multiply the tangent vectors by the imaginary unit i giving
18
the complex structure J. A Kähler manifold additionally has a Riemannian metric g which is
preserved by its complex structure:- g(JX, JY ) = g(X, Y ) , allowing one to deﬁne the Kähler
form:- w(X, Y ) = g(JX, JY )
This deﬁning property of a Kähler manifold is that this two form is closed i.e, dw = 0. [31].
Geometrically, this means that the complex, the metric and the symplectic structures all ﬁt
together consistently. Complex projective space why odd Betti numbers vanish on CP
N−1
is
the prototypical example of a compact Kähler manifold. Hodge theory is one of the major
consequences of the Kähler condition.
7 The Witten Index
Given a theory deﬁned with a Hilbert space H, the main concern is whether there exist
theories in H with zero-energy states. In supersymmetric theories, the energy E is greater
than or equal to the magnitude of the momentum |P| for any state. Zero-energy states must
therefore have P = 0.

8.1 BPS protection
Proposition 8.1 (BPS Protection). The signiﬁcance of BPS states for our work, lies in their
quantum protection. Consider a perturbative theory, where if we change the coupling
constant, a small SUSY preserving term gets added (or including quantum correction). The
key result is going to be the following:-
Let |ψ

non-perturbative theories, provided that the SUSY is unbroken.
(b). A short multiplet cannot become a long multiplet without a phase transition i.e, the
supermultiplet structure (the set of states and quantum numbers) cannot undergo a continuous
transformation.
(c). Any exact operator given by O = {Q, Λ} has a vanishing expectation value in a BPS state.
